claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr contains refractory elements with different atomic sizes.
Atomic-size mismatch in WTaTiVZr produces localized lattice distortions.
Localized lattice distortions promote nanoscale phase separation in WTaTiVZr.
Nanoscale segregated regions in WTaTiVZr act as strong dislocation-pinning centers.
The proposed pinning centers alter dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Lattice-distortion-induced phase separation and dislocation pinning govern the plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
Processing WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten under similar conditions will minimize microstructural variability in the comparison.
Identical high-temperature mechanical tests with in-situ characterization provide a controlled comparison between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
Solute or atomic-volume mismatch can contribute to strengthening in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Obstruction of dislocation mobility by the proposed pinning regions enhances the high-temperature yield strength of WTaTiVZr.
Excessively effective dislocation pinning may limit plastic strain and reduce toughness in WTaTiVZr.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will have higher yield strength than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will show more pronounced dislocation pinning than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit reduced plastic strain and potentially lower toughness than pure tungsten when pinning centers are sufficiently dense.
The high-temperature behavior of tungsten in plasma-facing applications has been extensively studied.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply above approximately 900 °C at strain rates where lattice distortions and nanoscale phase separation remain active.
The proposed mechanism may not dominate at low temperatures or at strain rates permitting substantial thermal recovery.
Comparable phase separation, pinning behavior, dislocation mobility, and stress-strain response in WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten would falsify the proposed mechanism.
